clue.text: Aunt Sally, say, is a legit target

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a game played at a fair; Aunt Sally is an old fairground game of throwing sticks at a dummy's head
second meaning: someone or something it is acceptable to attack or criticise

explanation.surface: Someone argues that the much-mocked Aunt Sally deserves whatever is thrown at her.
explanation.walkthrough: Aunt Sally reads as a person to be attacked, but here she is the literal fairground game; 'say' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names anyone legitimately open to attack, and literally a game played at a fairground.

clue.text: Cook sent in more soup

indicators.note: to cook is to doctor or falsify, so the following letters are tampered with and rearranged

parts.note: the three words taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: An instruction to a kitchen to send out more soup.
explanation.definitionFit: Minestrone is a thick Italian vegetable soup, an example of the general term.

clue.text: One cleric's free and brings back union

indicators.note: letters set free are released from their order and can be rearranged

parts.note: the words taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: A priest, newly at liberty, patches up a marriage or a divided church.
explanation.definitionFit: To reconcile estranged parties is to restore harmony between them, bringing them together again.

clue.text: Potty craze on the up over time

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece sitting over another comes first in the column
in a down clue, going up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a fad is a short-lived craze
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A silly trend keeps gaining popularity as time goes on.
explanation.definitionFit: Potty is British informal for slightly mad or foolish, the same sense as daft.

clue.text: Sham answer closing piece

parts.note: cod as an adjective means fake or mock, as in a cod accent
A is the standard abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: A bogus reply rounds off some piece of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: Cod meaning sham is British informal usage, as in cod philosophy.
explanation.definitionFit: A coda is the concluding passage of a musical work or the final section of anything.

clue.text: Two diamonds cut into little squares

parts.note: two separate words for diamonds follow
D abbreviates the card suit diamonds
ice is slang for diamonds

explanation.surface: A jeweller describes two gems being chopped into small square shapes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two diamonds' asks for two different renderings of the one word: the card-suit letter and the slang term.
explanation.definitionFit: To dice food is to chop it into small cubes, the cook's term for cutting it into little squares.

clue.text: Figure out the Devil will cover its head

indicators.note: something that covers another wraps around it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: the deuce is an old euphemism for the Devil, as in 'what the deuce'
the head, or first letter, of Devil

explanation.surface: Someone works out that Satan will hide his own head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The deuce' survives in exclamations like 'what the deuce?', where it stands in for the Devil; 'its head' points back to the word Devil.
explanation.definitionFit: To deduce is to reach a conclusion by reasoning, which is working something out.

clue.text: Spoof modelled on indignation

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece placed on another sits immediately before it

parts.note: an artist's model sat for the portrait
ire is anger or indignation

explanation.surface: A parody inspired by righteous anger.
explanation.definitionFit: A satire mocks its target, and a spoof is a humorous imitation that does the same.

clue.text: Intensely worried since end is changing

parts.note: as in 'long since' or 'long ago'

indicators.note: letters that are changing shift into a different order

parts.note: the two words taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: Someone is anxious because things are coming to an end and changing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Since' looks like a conjunction meaning because; here it is the adverb, as in years since or years ago.
explanation.definitionFit: Agonised describes someone tormented by anxiety or distress, deeply troubled.

clue.text: Cheese is skimpy, skipping it is fine

indicators.note: skipping something means passing over it, so that item is dropped from the word

parts.note: skimpy clothing is brief
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: A complaint that the cheese portion is mean, then a shrug that leaving it out is fine.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'skimpy, skipping fine': the word for skimpy loses its F.
explanation.definitionFit: Brie is a soft French cheese, an example of the general term.

clue.text: Ghastly rogue's auto is truly dreadful

indicators.note: something ghastly has been horribly mangled, so its letters are disordered

parts.note: the words taken letter by letter, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A villain's car is described as hideous and awful.
explanation.definitionFit: Outrageous means shockingly bad or excessive, which is what truly dreadful conveys.

clue.text: Reality is profitable Conservative admitted

indicators.note: someone admitted is let inside, so one piece enters another

parts.note: as in a fat contract, one that pays well
C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A political observation that a Tory confessed something lucrative was true.
explanation.definitionFit: A fact is something that actually is the case, a piece of reality rather than opinion.

clue.text: Who gets jittery near jam jar? One dealing with bar codes

indicators.note: one piece placed near another simply sits beside it in the answer

parts.note: jam jar is Cockney rhyming slang for car
one who dreads gets nervous

explanation.surface: A riddle about someone nervous beside a preserve pot, then a nod to scanning.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces appear in reverse order: the car comes first, the nervous person after. Cockney rhyming slang replaces a word with a phrase that rhymes with it.
explanation.definitionFit: A card reader is a device that reads encoded data from cards, the same job as scanning bar codes.

clue.text: Strange and mostly disagreeable dance

indicators.note: mostly means not all of it, so the word loses its final letter
the conjunction simply joins two pieces one after another

parts.note: rum is British informal for odd or strange
bad in the sense of unpleasant

explanation.surface: A dance described as weird and rather unpleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: The rumba is a Cuban ballroom dance, an example of the general term.

clue.text: You'll see this in redeveloped Seattle area for the most part

definitions.text: You'll see this in redeveloped Seattle area for the most part

indicators.note: redeveloped land is rebuilt in a new layout, so the letters are rearranged
only most of the word is used, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A comment on property visible across a rebuilt district of Seattle.
explanation.walkthrough: Area loses its final A, then joins Seattle in the anagram; the whole clue also describes what redevelopment produces.
explanation.definitionFit: Real estate is property in buildings and land, exactly what a redeveloped city area is made of.

clue.text: When draining depression changed into expectation

parts.note: as in 'as I arrived'

indicators.note: a word that has changed is reshaped into a different arrangement

parts.note: a sump is a pit or hollow into which liquid drains
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone's low mood, once it lifted, turned into hopefulness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draining depression' reads as easing gloom, but it is a hollow that collects drainage.
explanation.definitionFit: An assumption is something taken for granted or expected to be true.

clue.text: Rule out one who served with Oscar

indicators.note: one piece accompanied by another sits right beside it

parts.note: a vet, short for veteran, has served in the armed forces
Oscar is the radio alphabet code word for O

explanation.surface: Excluding a former soldier who served alongside someone called Oscar.
explanation.definitionFit: To veto a proposal is to forbid or reject it, ruling it out.

clue.text: Argument of large novel set in Highbury

parts.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
Jane Austen's novel Emma takes place in the village of Highbury

explanation.surface: A literary debate about a big book with a Highbury setting.
explanation.definitionFit: A lemma is a proposition assumed or proved within a larger argument, a step in logical reasoning.

clue.text: Buffet buddy's knocked back

indicators.note: something knocked back is sent the other way, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: buddy is pal, with the possessive S

explanation.surface: A friend's drinks at a buffet have been downed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buffet' tempts as a meal, but it is the verb meaning to strike; 'knocked back' suggests drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: To buffet someone is to hit them, and a slap is such a blow.

clue.text: Intimate friend to change, for example, nothing

parts.note: to alter is to change
e.g. is the abbreviation for 'for example'
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A close friend can change for nothing at all, it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: An alter ego, literally 'other self', is a trusted friend almost like a second self.

clue.text: Pud or similar to hold fragrance

parts.note: afters is British informal for dessert, and pud is short for pudding
to have is to hold or possess

explanation.surface: A dessert is supposed to contain some perfume.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, pud and afters are both everyday words for the dessert course.
explanation.definitionFit: Aftershave is a scented lotion men apply after shaving, so a kind of fragrance.

clue.text: Like one blooming loud Latin viva voce

parts.note: F is forte, the musical direction for loud
L is the standard abbreviation for Latin
a viva voce is an oral examination

explanation.surface: A flower described as loudly spouting Latin in a spoken exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' reads as a British mild oath intensifying loud; it is literal flowering.
explanation.definitionFit: Floral means relating to flowers, so like something in bloom.

clue.text: Tot's vocal power

indicators.note: vocal points to the voice, so the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: might is strength or power

explanation.surface: A small child has a powerful voice.
explanation.definitionFit: A mite is an affectionate word for a small child, a little one.

clue.text: Stupid clot with suntan finds someone giving advice

indicators.note: something stupid is muddled, so the letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sunburnt fool goes looking for someone to advise them.
explanation.walkthrough: A clot is British informal for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A consultant is a professional engaged to give expert advice.

clue.text: Schooner or the like from hotel with sample outside

indicators.note: one piece going outside wraps around the other

parts.note: a sip is a small taste
Hotel is the radio alphabet code word for H

explanation.surface: A glass of sherry served at a hotel, with a taste offered first.
explanation.walkthrough: A schooner is also a large sherry or beer glass, which suits the sipping surface; here it is the sailing vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: A schooner is a sailing vessel, an example of the wider class of seagoing craft.

clue.text: Assistance under Labour's opening show is put down

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece under another comes after it
the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of Labour
aid is help or assistance

explanation.surface: Help pledged at the start of a Labour political show is shelved.
explanation.definitionFit: Laid is the past participle of lay, meaning set down, as in laid on the table.

clue.text: Promote a punt, perhaps

parts.note: taken as written
a punt is a wager, one example of a bet

explanation.surface: Advocating a small gamble.
explanation.walkthrough: Punt tempts as a flat river boat or a kick; in British usage it is also a bet.
explanation.definitionFit: To abet is to encourage or support, especially wrongdoing, which promotes it.

clue.text: Flirt round Westminster's last traditionalist?

indicators.note: one piece going round another surrounds it

parts.note: to toy with someone is to flirt

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of Westminster

explanation.surface: A flirtation conducted around the Houses of Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition as an example: a Tory is a conservative, often a traditionalist. Tory is the everyday name for a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Conservatives, Tories in Britain, typically favour keeping traditional institutions and values.

clue.text: Seaside play about a luxurious hotel which doesn't close

indicators.note: one piece placed about another goes around it

parts.note: mime is wordless acting
taken as written

indicators.note: a word that never closes has no ending, so its final letter goes

parts.note: the Ritz is a famous luxury hotel in London

explanation.surface: A drama about a posh hotel by the coast that stays open all night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Which doesn't close' sounds like a 24-hour hotel; it means the hotel's name loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Maritime means relating to or by the sea, as in maritime provinces on the coast.

clue.text: With the ultimate in contempt unpleasant beasts scoff at this

indicators.note: the ultimate is the final one, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of contempt
as in a rough time

explanation.surface: Nasty animals jeer at something with utter disdain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoff at' reads as mock; it is British slang for eat greedily, and beasts eat from this.
explanation.definitionFit: A trough is the long open container from which farm animals eat or drink.
